newsitem.title: USA: Largest U.S. HMO considers partnership with unions.
newsitem.headline: Largest U.S. HMO considers partnership with unions.

text.p: Kaiser Permanente, the largest U.S. health maintenance organisation, said Thursday it would consider a partnership with its unions to give healthcare workers more say in decisions on patient treatment.

The agreement to negotiate a possible alliance was reached by Kaiser and the AFL-CIO, which represents about 55,000 workers at Kaiser. Although the two parties are just beginning talks, if an alliance were formed it would be the first national partnership between labour and management in the healthcare industry.

"We realise that we set the standard in the healthcare industry, and we're going to be far more successful if we work together," Kaiser Foundation Health Plan Chief Executive Officer, Dr. David Lawrence, said in a statement.

A spokeswoman for Kaiser said it had been considering the idea of a partnership with labour for the past two years, and had increasingly recognised it needed to change the way it operated to adapt to dramatic changes in the healthcare business.

As the largest HMO in the country, Kaiser is frequently the target of attacks on the besieged managed care industry. Critics say Kaiser is a profit-driven organisation that often denies patients the care they need in order to save costs.

Some other non-AFL-CIO unions, however, said they would not participate in negotiations. The California Nurses Asociation, which last week staged a one-day strike to protest pay cuts and staff reductions, said it found Kaiser's motives suspect.
The union said it had been advocating better patient care for the past three years, and had been unable to stop continued cuts in staffing at Kaiser.
